newsitem.title: FRANCE: France urges less US leadership, more partnership.
newsitem.headline: France urges less US leadership, more partnership.

text.p: French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette, acknowledging differences with Washington on the role of Europe in NATO and the Middle East, said that he would prefer more partnership and less leadership from the United States.
In an interview with Time magazine published on Monday, de Charette denied that France and Washington were at odds over Africa and that he had snubbed outgoing Secretary of State Warren Christopher.
He said Washington had understood that a strong and united Europe was in its interests but a dispute over a bigger European share of NATO regional commands had yet to be resolved.

"Our ambition is for Europe to assume its full responsibilities, play its full role. We would prefer more partnership and less leadership from the United States -- a dialogue between equals," he said.

De Charette said he was open to alternative proposals to its stipulation that a European take over NATO's southern command, a demand rejected by Washington which wants to hold on to a job currently overseeing the U.S. Mediterranean Sixth Fleet.

"If there is to be a new alliance, in which Europe plays a role, there must be a new sharing of responsibilities...But a situation where the Americans hold three commands to Europe's one is hardly what we consider sharing responsibility," he said.
De Charette said the demand was European rather than French, and Europe was not seeking to take command of the Sixth Fleet.
He denied that he had snubbed Christopher by walking out of a farewell toast in honour of the American at NATO headquarters in Brussels last month.
"Frankly, it came as a considerable surprise to me because the whole thing was a lie - totally," he said.
He said he had a very cordial and confident relationship with Christopher despite some "intense moments" over the past 18 months.

De Charette also acknowledged differences over the Middle East, a region where both Europeans and Americans have major interests, and called on Washington to let the Europeans take on a bigger role in the Middle East peace process.
"For the time being, the Americans have a role in the peace process...That's fine, and very useful for all concerned. But we think that Europe and the United States must work hand-in-hand," he said.
He denied that recent sharp exchanges over Africa meant Paris and Washington were involved in a confrontation or even competition over the continent.

"We have converging interests: the stabilisation and development of Africa, the resolution of the crisis in the Great Lakes region. There is no French or American private domain in Africa or anywhere else," he said.
Paris has accused Washington of showing interest in Africa only at election time to sway black American voters.

The two countries have been at odds over the appointment of Ghana's Kofi Annan as United Nations Secretary General, and over France's insistence on sending a multinational force to ensure relief for refugees in eastern Zaire.
